start: the unexamined life is not worth living
context: Socrates says this at his trial in Athens, having been offered the chance to live if he stops questioning people. He chooses the examined life, even at the cost of his own.
prompt: What part of your life have you stopped questioning?

start: he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows
context: Socrates explains why the oracle called him the wisest man in Athens: not because he knew more, but because he was honest about the limits of what he knew.
prompt: Where are you most certain — and what would it cost to be less so?

start: the beginning is the most important part of any work
context: Said in a discussion of how to educate the young: early impressions shape everything that follows. The point applies just as well to habits, projects and days.
prompt: How do you want to begin what comes next?

start: wonder is the feeling of a philosopher
context: Socrates says this to the young Theaetetus, who admits he is dizzy with puzzlement. Confusion is not a failure; it is where real thinking starts.
prompt: What has made you wonder recently?

context: Socrates shocks his companions by arguing that doing wrong damages the soul far more than being wronged does.
prompt: Is there a wrong you could avoid doing, even at some cost to yourself?

start: be of good cheer about death, and know of a certainty
context: Socrates' words to the jurors who voted to acquit him. A good person's integrity cannot be taken from them by anything that happens.
prompt: What in you can no misfortune touch?

start: The difficulty, my friends, is not to avoid death
context: Sentenced to die, Socrates observes that wrongdoing is the swifter pursuer. His accusers, he says, have been overtaken by it.
prompt: What wrong is easier to fall into than you'd like to admit?

start: The hour of departure has arrived
context: The final words of Socrates' defence, spoken with calm to the court that has condemned him.
prompt: How would you want to speak if these were your last words?

start: I would rather die having spoken after my manner
context: Socrates refuses to beg for mercy or bring his weeping children to court. He would rather die true to himself than live by betraying himself.
prompt: Where are you speaking in someone else's manner to stay comfortable?

start: For I do nothing but go about persuading you all
context: Socrates describes the message he has spent his life repeating to the people of Athens: care first for your soul.
prompt: How much of your care goes to your soul, compared with your possessions?

start: not life, but a good life, is to be chiefly valued
context: In prison, his friend Crito urges Socrates to escape. Socrates insists the question is not how to live longer but how to live well.
prompt: Are you living a long life, or a good one?

start: Then we ought not to retaliate or render evil for evil
context: Socrates admits this view has never been popular. He holds to it anyway, even facing death.
prompt: Whom are you tempted to repay in kind?

start: we must not regard what the many say of us
context: Public opinion is not the measure of right and wrong. Socrates asks what someone who truly understands would say, and what the truth would say.
prompt: Whose opinion are you living by, the many's or the truth's?

start: we shall be better and braver and less helpless
context: Socrates is unsure of much, but of this he is certain: believing inquiry is worthwhile makes us better people.
prompt: What question have you given up on that is still worth asking?

start: there is a victory and defeat
context: From Plato's last and longest dialogue. The fiercest war is the one fought within each person.
prompt: What inner battle are you fighting right now?

start: I would rather that my lyre should be inharmonious
context: Socrates would rather the whole world disagree with him than live in disagreement with himself.
prompt: Where are you at odds with yourself?

start: Let us, then, take the argument as our guide
context: The closing words of the Gorgias. After a long and heated argument, Socrates concludes simply: practise justice and every virtue.
prompt: What would it mean to follow the argument wherever it leads?

start: Behold! human beings living in a underground den
context: The opening of the Allegory of the Cave. Prisoners mistake shadows on a wall for reality; philosophy is the slow, painful turn toward the light.
prompt: What shadows might you be mistaking for the real thing?

near: they will creep into the city unobserved
start: Wealth, I said, and poverty
context: Socrates names two dangers to a healthy community, and to a healthy soul: too much and too little.
prompt: Has abundance or scarcity been shaping your character lately?

context: Plato's view of education: learning forced on us does not last. Learning through play reveals who we really are.
prompt: What would you love to learn if no one were making you?

start: old age has a great sense of calm and freedom
context: The elderly Cephalus, at the opening of the Republic, finds that age has freed him from the tyranny of his passions.
prompt: What passion would you be glad to be free of?

start: he who is of a calm and happy nature
context: Cephalus again: what makes a life heavy is not age but temperament.
prompt: What in your temperament makes life lighter, or heavier?

start: the power and capacity of learning exists in the soul already
context: Education, for Plato, is not pouring knowledge into an empty vessel but turning the whole soul toward the light.
prompt: What understanding is already in you, waiting to be turned toward?

start: In heaven, I replied, there is laid up a pattern of it
end: set his own house in order.
context: The ideal city may never exist on earth. But anyone can use it as a pattern for ordering their own life.
prompt: What pattern are you ordering your inner house by?

start: Then to injure a friend or any one else is not the act of a just man
context: Against the common view that justice means helping friends and harming enemies, Socrates argues that a just person harms no one.
prompt: Is there anyone you feel entitled to harm?

start: he sets in order his own inner life
context: Plato's definition of justice in the soul: each part doing its own work, in harmony, like notes in a scale.
prompt: What would it take to be at peace with yourself today?

start: He who is the real tyrant, whatever men may think, is the real slave
context: The tyrant seems to have everything, but is ruled by desires he can never satisfy.
prompt: Which of your desires rules you more than you rule it?

start: No man would keep his hands off what was not his own
context: From the story of the Ring of Gyges, which makes its wearer invisible. Glaucon challenges Socrates: would anyone stay just if no one could see?
prompt: What would you do differently if no one could ever see?

start: human nature was originally one and we were a whole
context: From Aristophanes' speech: humans were once whole beings, split in two, and love is the longing to be whole again.
prompt: What makes you feel whole?

start: This, my dear Socrates,' said the stranger
context: The priestess Diotima teaches Socrates that love climbs from beautiful bodies to beautiful souls, ideas, and finally beauty itself.
prompt: Where did you notice beauty today?

end: between the wise and the ignorant.
context: Love, in Diotima's account, is neither wise nor ignorant but always reaching: the very definition of a philosopher.
prompt: What are you reaching for that you don't yet have?

start: give me beauty in the inward soul
context: Socrates' prayer at the end of the Phaedrus: inner beauty, harmony between inner and outer life, and only as much wealth as a temperate person can carry.
prompt: How could your outward life better match your inward one?

parts: the human charioteer drives his in a pair
context: Plato's image of the soul as a charioteer with two horses, one noble and one unruly. Reason must steer both.
prompt: Which of your horses has been pulling harder lately?

start: this discovery of yours will create forgetfulness
context: An Egyptian king warns the inventor of writing that it will weaken memory and give only the appearance of wisdom. The worry sounds familiar today.
prompt: What do you know only because it is stored somewhere, not in you?

start: How singular is the thing called pleasure
context: Socrates, his chains just removed on the day of his death, rubs his leg and reflects on how pleasure and pain always follow each other.
prompt: Which pleasure in your life always seems to bring its pain?

start: Lest we become misologists
context: After an argument collapses, Socrates warns against giving up on reasoning altogether, just as disappointment can turn people against humanity.
prompt: Where has disappointment made you cynical?

start: of all the men of his time whom I have known
context: The last line of the Phaedo, Phaedo's tribute to Socrates after his death.
prompt: What would you want those who knew you to say?
